## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.67670.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.67670.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Acceptance summary:

Here, Razzauti and Laurent show that membrane proteins in the cilia of C. elegans sensory neurons can be released in extracellular vesicles (EVs) produced by two distinct regions of the cilium. EVs released from one of these sites can be taken up by an adjacent glial cell, though the functional significance of this remains speculative. Importantly, the authors find that EV release is dramatically enhanced when ciliary membrane proteins are overexpressed, suggesting that this process acts as a safety valve that protects cilium integrity.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Ectosome uptake by glia sculpts Caenorhabditis elegans sensory cilia" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Doug Portman as the Reviewing Editor and Piali Sengupta as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Maxence V Nachury (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers and editors have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

We feel that your paper reports a number of interesting findings that advance our understanding of the biology of cilia and glia in C. elegans. However, there are two areas in which additional experiments would be necessary in a revised submission. In addition, each reviewer has provided additional comments and suggestions that we ask you to consider as you prepare a resubmission.

Essential revisions:

(1) Concerns about overexpression artifacts. Aside from the DiI experiments, all evidence for EV release and glial uptake relies on the overexpression of cilium proteins. This leads to questions about the extent to which your findings reflect typical neuronal/glial functions, or, rather, are observed only when cilia are disrupted by protein overexpression. The best way to address this would be to carry out additional experiments using an endogenously-tagged cargo protein. As pointed out by Reviewer #1 below, such a reagent has been published (GCY-22), so you would not necessarily need to generate any new transgenes.

(2) Concerns about interpretation of the experiments in which AMsh function is disrupted. As reviewer #2 notes, expression of dyn-1(dn) in AMsh, or loss of ced-10, might compromise AMsh function in ways that affect additional functions besides its ability to take up ciliary EVs. For this reason, it cannot be definitively concluded that the changes you see in NRE morphology and behavior in AMsh::dyn-1(dn) or ced-10 mutants are specific consequences of problems with EV uptake. Further, your experiments do not definitively show that EV uptake relies on the cell-autonomous function of ced-10 in AMsh, so these phenotypes could be indirect. These issues can be addressed with the following experiments.

(a) examine AMsh morphology in AMsh::dyn-10(dn) and/or ced-10 and AMsh::ced-10 animals. If AMsh morphology is grossly disrupted, this would indicate that its function may be more generally disrupted.

(b) similarly, examine AWC NRE morphology in these animals. Even if AMsh morphology is intact, its function can be generally compromised. In these cases, the AWC cilium typically collapses.

(c) carry out ced-10; AMsh::ced-10 rescue experiments, examining EV uptake, ASER NRE morphology, and salt chemotaxis. This would provide a second line of evidence that links EV uptake by AMsh to maintenance of cilium morphology and neuronal function.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Are the EVs that end up in glial cells ectosomes? Do they originate from the cilium proper or from the plasma membrane or are they exosomes? The intro (line 63-67) quotes Barr lab papers showing that mutation of MVB biogenesis genes STAM (ESCRT-0), MVB12 (ESCRT-I) or ALIX does not affect production of PKD2 EV by CEM neurons. Are ILVs absent from the MVB in these mutants? The point being raised is whether the hypothesis of MVB origin has been satisfactorily rejected. The question becomes relevant when one considers that the tetraspanins chosen by the authors are known markers of exosomes. In particular CD63 is a marker of exosomes but not of ectosomes as CD63 is enriched in ILVs of late endosomes but not present at the plasma membrane. Leaving open the possibility that the material is transferred via exosomes would be wise.

The most direct evidence for ectosomes budding from a ciliated neuron and engulfed by a support cell is presented in Video 6. In this video, where is the cilium and where are the microvilli? Can one determine the origin of the EV?

The use of overexpression system for the ciliary signaling receptors results in their localization to both cilia and PCMC and the dilation of the PCMC. It is therefore conceivable that the observed transfer of material from ciliated neuron to support cell is caused by receptor overexpression. The strong signal at the PCMC for all membrane proteins tested (except SRBC-64) leads one to wonder whether excess signaling receptors may accumulate at the PCMC and become shed. Figure 3C shows that SRBC-64 is present at similar levels in cilia and at the PCMC, unlike the other markers used in the study that are more highly enriched in the PCMC than in cilia. The fact that SRBC-64 is the only receptor that does not end in vesicles inside the support cell casts doubt on the ciliary origin of the EVs. The fluorescent signals also appear to be the weakest for this protein, suggesting that SRBC64 is the least overexpressed of all proteins tested. The result that EV transfer from ciliated neuron to support cell is increased when cilia are absent strengthen the interpretation that the material that is transferred is not of ciliary origin.

The expression of dominant negative dynamin in AMsh is interesting. Filopodial-looking extensions originating from the ASER are now detected more frequently. This suggests that these filopodial extensions from the ciliated neuron are phagocytosed by the AMsh. The images shown suggest that the filopodial extension do not originate from the cilium itself but rather from the PCMC or the distal dendrite. The strong reduction in TSP7 transfer from AFD to AMsh in mutant that lacks actin-base protrusion suggests that actin-based protrusion are the relevant entities for material sending by the donor cell.

It would be good to discuss the model that actin protrusions emanating from the PCMC are responsible for the material transfer from neurons to glial cells. Given the strong supportive evidence for actin protrusions playing a role in the process under study, these protrusions could be included in the model in Figure 8. The model should also show PCMC and cilia proper.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. Release of EVs from sensory neurons and their uptake by surrounding cells has been previously described and should be cited (Melentijevic et al., Nature 2017).

2. The statement that "DiI passively diffuses in lipid membranes it contacts" is misleading. Several externally exposed neurons do not stain with DiI.

3. The statement that "most of the glial cells (46 out of 50) associate with groups of ciliated neurons to form sensory organs named sensilla" is confusing. All 50 glia do this.

4. The statement that the authors observed "barely detectable basal ectosomes… suggesting [their] size [is] close to the light diffraction limit of conventional confocal microscopes" is confusing. The light diffraction limit is related to resolution, that is, the ability to distinguish two objects as being distinct from each other. The authors seem to be referring to brightness which is not necessarily related to size.

5. The word "length" is misspelled in all figures where it appears.

Only as a note to the authors: I find the pseudo-typeset formatting to be very difficult to review. I would greatly prefer a simple text document with full-page figures and legends at the end. I understand that others may feel differently.

claims.claim: EVs remain produced by AFD receptive endings in the absence of AMsh glia.
claims.source: Our previous results highlight the active role of neurons for basal ectosome production. However, ectosomes do not accumulate in the amphid sensilla of hermaphrodites, highlighting their efficient clearance by AMsh. This clearance could occur passively by phagocytosis of passing-by EVs; in this case, an AMsh endocytic defect would lead to EV accumulation in the lumen of the amphid sensilla, between amphid cilia and AMsh. Alternatively, as PCMC and AMsh plasma membranes are closely associated, PCMC ectocytosis might occur simultaneously to glial phagocytosis. Such mechanism would facilitate ectosome clearance and limit the risk of ectosomes accumulating between cilia and glia. In this case, an AMsh endocytic defect would lead to abnormal cilia shape caused by unsolved ectosome uptake. To test these two models, we reduced AMsh endocytic activity by overexpressing cell-specifically a dominant negative construct for DYN-1. In human macrophages, Dynamin 2 is recruited early during phagosome formation and contributes to phagosome scission from plasma membrane (Marie-Anais et al., 2016). Dynamin 2 dominant negative mutation (K44A) abolishes GTP binding activity and disturb pseudopod extension (Gold et al., 1999). Similar dominant mutations in its C. elegans ortholog dyn-1(G40E and K46A) disturb engulfment rate, RAB-5 recruitment, phagosome maturation, and degradation (Kinchen et al., 2008; He et al., 2010). As expected, if ASER PCMC ectocytosis was coordinated with AMsh phagocytosis, we observed abnormal filopodia-like protrusions still attached to the ASER PCMC when DYN-1(K46A) was overexpressed in AMsh (Figure 7A). We never observed EVs accumulating between ASER and AMsh. Instead, many tiny vesicles were observed in the vicinity of ASER cilium, sometimes generating string of pearls within AMsh cytoplasm (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A′). To assess this non-cell-autonomous effect of AMsh::DYN-1(K46A) on other amphid neurons, we examined the morphology of ASH, AFD, and AWC NREs. In agreement with ASER results, we saw expression of DYN-1(K46A) in AMsh induced abnormal filopodia-like protrusions still attached to ASH PCMC (Figure 7B). Expression of DYN-1(K46A) in AMsh induced abnormal AWC cilia where the wing-like sheets are replaced by branches; filopodia-like protrusions still attached to AWC PCMC were observed in 11 of the 14 AWC cilia imaged (Figure 7C). Expression of DYN-1(K46A) in AMsh induced abnormal AFD microvilli architecture as well as abnormal filopodia-like protrusions attached to AFD PCMC (Figure 7D). We never observed EVs accumulating between ASH, AFD, AWC, AFD NREs, and AMsh, suggesting that the EVs produced are not accumulating outside the glia. Instead, we observed filopodia-like protrusion remaining attached to the PCMC. Expression of DYN-1(K46A) disturbs a whole set of AMsh functions, including phagocytosis. Therefore, filopodia-like protrusion originating from PCMC might correspond to ectosomes not readily pinched. We observed that DYN-1(K46A) affected AMsh position and shape, suggesting that it modifies AMsh cell biology. Previously, it was shown that ablation of AMsh, cell-specific expression of RAB-1(S25N) causing exocytosis defect or a pros-1 mutation causing secretome defect all induced severe truncation of AWC and AFD NREs (Bacaj et al., 2008; Singhvi et al., 2016; Wallace et al., 2016). We observed severe microvilli truncation in ~10% of AFD NRE, and we did not observe truncations of AWC wing cilia.

results.result: DiI-stained neuronal membranes are exported from amphid neurons to AMsh glia in an ATP-dependent manner. DiI staining of neurons and glia occurs rapidly (20 min), with DiI-stained vesicles observed within AMsh cytoplasm and accumulating in the AMsh 'pocket'. Time-lapse imaging shows vesicles are produced at ciliated endings and flow toward AMsh. Sodium azide treatment, which depletes ATP, blocks DiI transfer from neurons to glia, but transfer resumes after washout.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C39 provide converging evidence from DiI staining kinetics (C28), imaging of vesicles in AMsh (C29-C32), and ATP depletion experiments (C33-C39) that collectively demonstrate ATP-dependent transfer of neuronal membrane to glia. The sodium azide experiments provide strong evidence for the ATP-dependence of the transfer process, with appropriate controls and washout experiments.

results.result: TSP-6 and TSP-7 (C. elegans orthologs of mammalian CD9 and CD63) are enriched in ciliary membrane compartments and are exported from amphid neurons to EVs in the amphid pore and/or AMsh glia. When overexpressed in specific neurons (ASER, ASH, ASI, AFD), these tetraspanin markers localize to cilia and PCMC and are found in EVs within AMsh cytoplasm. Export occurs in a lateralized manner (e.g., ASER to AMshR only) and is observed across developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C40-C67 provide extensive imaging evidence from multiple neuron types showing that TSP-6 and TSP-7 localize to cilia (C48-C50) and are exported to EVs in AMsh (C51-C63). The bioinformatic identification of TSP-6/TSP-7 as CD9/CD63 orthologs (C45) is appropriate, and the lateralized export pattern (C53-C54) provides strong evidence for PCMC as the source of basal EVs. The developmental time-course (C64-C65) supports continuous export.

results.result: Ciliary ectosomes bud from two locations: the cilia tip (leading to environmental release) and the PCMC (leading to glial uptake). Live imaging of IL2 neurons shows outward budding of ectosomes varying from <250 nm to ~2 μm diameter from the cilia tip, with variable scission timing. Ectosomes from PCMC are captured by ILsh/ILso glia. Cargo sorting into ectosomes depends on cargo localization at the time of budding, with PCMC-enriched markers more likely to enter basal ectosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C68-C89 provide direct live imaging evidence (Videos 2-5) of ectosome formation from two ciliary locations with distinct fates. The observations of ectosome size variability (C76-C77, C85), cargo-dependent sorting (C78-C79, C87), and differential capture by glia (C81-C82, C88-C89) are well-documented. The time-lapse data provide strong mechanistic insights into ectosome biogenesis dynamics.

results.result: Most overexpressed ciliary membrane proteins (GCY-8, SRTX-1, GCY-22) can be loaded into ciliary EVs and exported to AMsh, with the exception of SRBC-64. GCY-22-wrmScarlet produces large (~1 μm) EVs that bud from ASER PCMC over 6-25 min, with the entire budding process occurring in close contact with AMsh. The budding dynamics can be resolved and recorded in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C107 demonstrate that multiple ciliary receptors can enter EVs when overexpressed (C92-C94, C99), with appropriate negative control (SRBC-64, C96). The live imaging of GCY-22 budding (C101-C105, Video 6) provides direct evidence of the mechanism. The observation that SRBC-64 does not enter EVs (C107) is important for understanding cargo selectivity, though the authors appropriately note detection limits as a caveat.

results.result: Mutations in IFT machinery (osm-3, che-3, bbs-8, unc-101) lead to cargo accumulation in specific ciliary compartments and alter ectocytosis patterns. In osm-3 and che-3 mutants, GCY-22-GFP accumulates in PCMC and basal ectocytosis to AMsh increases ~4-fold. In bbs-8 mutants, apical ectocytosis increases ~3-fold and ciliary GCY-22-GFP levels decrease. In unc-101 mutants, GCY-22 fails to accumulate in cilia and ectocytosis is abolished. These results suggest ectocytosis acts as a safeguard mechanism to reduce cargo accumulation when IFT is disrupted.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C108-C135 provide systematic analysis of ectocytosis in multiple IFT mutants with complementary phenotypes. The osm-3/che-3 data (C118-C125) show PCMC accumulation correlates with increased basal ectocytosis, while bbs-8 data (C128-C132) show increased apical ectocytosis. The unc-101 data (C113-C115) provide important negative control showing ectocytosis requires cargo trafficking to cilia. The use of both overexpression and knock-in strains strengthens the conclusions. Quantitative data support the ~3-4 fold increases claimed.

results.result: Endogenously tagged TSP-6-wrmScarlet (knock-in) is expressed in multiple amphid neurons (ASK, ADF, ASJ, ASI, ASH, AWA, AWC) and shows physiological ectocytosis to both the amphid pore (~1.4 events/animal) and AMsh. In IFT mutants (osm-3, che-3, bbs-8), ectocytosis patterns mirror those observed with GCY-22-GFP: increased basal ectocytosis in osm-3/che-3 (~4-fold) and increased apical ectocytosis in bbs-8 (~3-fold). This confirms that ectocytosis contributes to reducing pathological cargo accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C146 provide critical validation using endogenous TSP-6 levels (knock-in) rather than overexpression, demonstrating physiological ectocytosis (C137-C139). The replication of IFT mutant phenotypes (C140-C142) with TSP-6 knock-in strengthens the conclusion that ectocytosis is a general response to cargo accumulation. The consistency between GCY-22 and TSP-6 results across multiple mutants provides strong support for the safeguard mechanism hypothesis.

results.result: Cargo composition affects ectosome budding dynamics and size. GCY-22 overexpression causes PCMC expansion and produces large (~1 μm) EVs that bud slowly (~1 event/14.66 min), while TSP-6 overexpression does not cause PCMC expansion and produces small (<500 nm) EVs that bud frequently (~1 event/1 min). Co-expression experiments show EVs carrying both cargoes have intermediate size (~600-700 nm), suggesting cargo interactions influence EV diameter.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C161 provide quantitative evidence that cargo identity affects EV size and budding kinetics (C152-C154). The comparison of PCMC expansion between GCY-22 and TSP-6 overexpression (C147, C151) and with mutants (C148-C149) is appropriate. The co-expression experiment (C157-C159) showing intermediate EV size provides strong evidence for cargo-dependent effects on budding dynamics. However, the mechanism remains speculative (C156, C160), which the authors appropriately acknowledge.

results.result: Basal ectosome production is inherent to neurons rather than driven by glial pruning. In ttx-1 mutants lacking AFD microvilli, TSP-7 export to AMsh still occurs but is reduced. In dyf-7 mutants with ectopically located AFD-AMsh contacts, TSP-7 export continues normally. In AMsh-ablated animals, EVs are still produced by AFD and are taken up by alternative cells (hypoderm, neurons), demonstrating that glial phagocytosis is secondary to neuronal EV production.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C177 provide strong evidence that neurons autonomously produce ectosomes. The ttx-1 experiments (C169-C171) show microvilli are important but not required, while dyf-7 experiments (C172-C174) show proper sensilla structure is not required. The AMsh ablation experiments (C175-C177) provide the most direct evidence that EV production is neuron-autonomous, with EVs redirected to other cell types in the absence of glia. This effectively rules out an active glial pruning model.

results.result: Expression of dominant-negative DYN-1(K46A) in AMsh disrupts glial phagocytosis and causes abnormal filopodia-like protrusions attached to the PCMC of ASER, ASH, AWC, and AFD neurons. This correlates with impaired sensory function in ASER and ASH but not AWC and AFD. The results suggest that glial phagocytosis is required to maintain cilia structure and function for a subset of neurons, with neurons and glia cooperating to remove basal ectosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C183 provide evidence that disrupting glial phagocytosis affects cilia morphology (C178) and sensory function (C179) for some neurons. The observation of filopodia-like protrusions rather than accumulated EVs supports the model of coupled budding-phagocytosis (C162). However, the differential effects on neuron types (C180-C181) and the pleiotropic effects of DYN-1(K46A) on AMsh biology complicate interpretation. The authors appropriately note these caveats and contrast with more severe phenotypes in other AMsh mutants (C182).

results.result: The authors propose that EV budding from cilia subcompartments acts as a safeguard mechanism to remove excess ciliary material when IFT is disrupted. Ectocytosis is constitutive of most or all C. elegans sensory cilia and contributes to maintaining appropriate cilia composition, structure, and function, acting as an alternative to IFT-mediated trafficking.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C193, and C195 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript. The safeguard mechanism hypothesis is well-supported by the systematic analysis of IFT mutants showing increased ectocytosis correlates with cargo accumulation (Results 5-6), the demonstration of physiological ectocytosis with knock-in strains (Result 6), and the evidence that ectocytosis is neuron-autonomous (Result 8). While the term 'safeguard' implies a protective function that is not directly tested (e.g., no rescue experiments), the correlative evidence is strong and the model is reasonable.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on cilia biology, IFT machinery, C. elegans as a model system, and the anatomy of the amphid sensilla. This includes established knowledge about cilia structure and function, IFT-mediated trafficking, the role of glia in sensory organs, and the specific organization of C. elegans amphid neurons and glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C9-C24 provide appropriate background and context, supported by citations to prior literature (C1, C12-C17, C23, C26) and established knowledge (C9-C11, C18-C22, C24). These claims accurately represent the current understanding of cilia biology and C. elegans anatomy.

results.result: The authors discuss parallels between their findings and other systems, including exophers in C. elegans touch neurons, photoreceptor disc shedding in mammals, and potential signaling functions of ciliary EVs. They speculate that ciliary ectosomes may have additional roles in neuron-glia communication beyond disposal.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C192 provide appropriate context from prior literature (C184-C186, C188) and reasonable speculation about potential functions (C189-C190, C192). However, these are primarily discussion points rather than results from the current study. The speculation about signaling functions (C189-C190, C192) is not directly tested and remains hypothetical.
